title: Dawn now comes one hour after the first bell. This Alberta school is handing out reflectors to keep kids safe
summary: Elementary schools in Brooks, Alta., are handing out reflective tags for students to wear on backpacks as they walk to school or to the bus in much darker conditions this winter — the first after…

image.caption: A neon green tag appears on a school backpack in Brooks, Alta., where the Grasslands School Division has distributed the reflective markers to students who may walk to school in pre-dawn conditions following and end to time-change. (Grasslands School Division)

blocks.text: Calgary

Elementary schools in Brooks, Alta., are handing out reflective tags for students to wear on backpacks as they walk to school or to the bus in much darker conditions this winter — the first after Alberta ended the practice of turning back clocks in the fall. Parents are welcoming the move.
Dawn comes one hour after first bell in Brooks, Alta.
Jacqui Alexander noticed it a few weeks ago on the school bus route she drives in Brooks, Alta. — it was getting light much later than usual after Alberta did away with time-change this month.
"As a bus driver… it's sort of right there in front of you — all these kids are walking to the bus stops and walking to school in the pitch black," she told CBC News.
"I had actually gone out to the dollar store and got reflective tape to put on my [own] kids' backpacks."
While Armstrong took matters into her own hands, she's pleased this week that the public school division in her city handed out small reflective backpack tags to all elementary students.
She said just a glint of light can alert motorists to kids walking to school in pre-dawn hours — a change from years past when clocks fell back an hour each fall.
"Even just the smallest thing makes a difference."

While there have been no accidents reported, administrators with Grasslands School Division in Brooks say they noticed the dim light when students arrive in the morning, and began hearing concern from parents.
Adjusting to later sunrise

The high-visibility patch — about the size of the flat side of a hockey puck and costing about $1 each — is a way to improve visibility on dark mornings. It also gives students and parents a physical reminder to keep safety in mind, said superintendent Scott Brandt.
"It seemed like a cool idea that wasn't that expensive," said Brandt, whose office distributed 1,500 tags this week for students in Kindergarten through Grade 6 classes in 14 city and rural schools.
"I just ordered another 1,000 and we'll get them out to the junior high [students] this week."
A reflective tag could alert drivers to the presence of school kids during darker morning commutes this winter, a southern Alberta school is hoping. (Grasslands School Division)
He credits a British Columbia school board for coming up with the idea, and since then other Alberta school districts have contacted him looking to copy the idea.
"I'm not surprised," said Brandt. "I'm sure everyone is noticing the same thing we are — it's just so dark in the morning."
Sun up well after the bell

This week, the sun is fully up at about 9 a.m. in Brooks, located about 190 kilometres east of Calgary. That is about 50 minutes after the earliest opening bell at Grassland schools. Many students walk to bus stops or school much earlier.
On the shortest day of the year, Dec. 21, dawn will only break in Brooks at 8:47 a.m. ahead of full sunrise at 9:26 a.m., according to the National Research Council's sun calculator for cities.
On the same day, the sun will set at about 4:30 p.m. Each is one hour later on the clock compared to before the province moved to "Alberta Time" this month.
Adjusting to new reality, say parents

Alexander was one who welcomed the change to more light in afternoons, but now has a mixed feelings and thinks people will need to adjust to driving until mornings get brighter as days get longer in January.
"I think it's a big change, and people hate change," she said. "But maybe we just get used to it and adapt, and then it's fine."

blocks.text: Similarly, school parent council member Sydney Webber drops off her two kids at school, and felt uneasy approaching school zones that were full of activity in different, darker morning conditions.
"It's honestly hard to see the kids," she told CBC News. "So I was very glad to see that our school district took the initiative to grab those reflector keychains for their backpacks."
Brandt said the division is also now evaluating the crosswalks and street lighting near its schools. It may have been adequate when the sun rose earlier, but now may need upgrading, he said.
Grasslands is also planning to bring in local RCMP officers to talk with students about traffic safety.
"If we can help our kids just be a little bit more visible and safe coming to school and going home at the end of the day, then it's a real small investment for the benefit of our kids," said Brandt.
